question: Two days after undergoing an emergency laparotomy following a motor vehicle collision, a 37-year-old man has increased thirst. Examination shows dry mucous membranes and decreased skin turgor. A review of his chart shows his urine output to be in excess of his fluid intake. Laboratory studies show a serum sodium concentration of 151 mEq/L and urine osmolality of 110 mOsmol/kg H2O. One hour after the administration of desmopressin, the serum sodium concentration is 146 mEq/L and urine osmolality is 400 mOsmol/kg H2O. One week later, his laboratory values are within normal limits. This patient's condition was most likely caused by damage to which of the following structures?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Damage to posterior pituitary -> decreased secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) -> decreased water reabsorption in the kidneys -> increased urine output -> dehydration symptoms -> increased thirst, dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor -> laboratory findings of hypernatremia and concentrated urine -> administration of desmopressin (ADH analog) -> increased water reabsorption in the kidneys -> normalization of serum sodium concentration and urine osmolality -> resolution of symptoms -> 95%
analysis: The patient is presenting with symptoms of diabetes insipidus, specifically central diabetes insipidus. The increased thirst, polyuria, high serum sodium concentration, and low urine osmolality are indicative of this condition. The response to desmopressin, a synthetic form of vasopressin, further supports the diagnosis. Damage to the posterior pituitary, which is responsible for producing and releasing vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone), is the likely cause of central diabetes insipidus in this case.
